summary: Chinese has no words for ‘my, your, his’: the personal pronoun + the particle 的 does it — 我的书 ‘my book’, 你的钥匙 ‘your key’, 他们的房子 ‘their house’. 的 links any owner to a thing (老师的书 ‘the teacher’s book’). With close family, one’s home and one’s own group the 的 is usually dropped: 我妈妈 ‘my mother’, 我家 ‘my family, my home’, 我们老师 ‘our teacher’.

head: father’s side
mother’s side
rows: 伯伯 (older than father), 叔叔 (younger)
堂哥 堂姐 堂弟 堂妹 (children of 伯伯 / 叔叔)
表哥 表姐 表弟 表妹 (also the children of 姑姑)
blocks.caption: The family system: every relative is named by side, sex and age

notes.text: English uncle, aunt and cousin cover all of these; Chinese names each one by side, sex and age: ‘my uncle’ has five translations (伯伯, 叔叔, 舅舅, 姑父, 姨父).

Turkish makes the same split by side: amca (father’s brother) ~ 伯伯 / 叔叔, dayı (mother’s brother) ~ 舅舅, hala (father’s sister) ~ 姑姑, teyze (mother’s sister) ~ 阿姨 / 姨妈. Chinese adds the age of the father’s brothers.
Hindi splits like Chinese, even by age: ताऊ (father’s elder brother) ~ 伯伯, चाचा (father’s younger brother) ~ 叔叔, मामा ~ 舅舅, बुआ ~ 姑姑, मौसी ~ 阿姨 / 姨妈.
Arabic separates ʿamm / ʿamma (father’s brother / sister) from khāl / khāla (mother’s brother / sister), like 叔叔 / 姑姑 vs 舅舅 / 阿姨; Chinese also splits the father’s brothers by age.
Persian amu / amme (father’s side) and dāyi / khāle (mother’s side) make the same split as 叔叔 / 姑姑 and 舅舅 / 阿姨; Chinese also splits the father’s brothers by age (伯伯 / 叔叔).
English brother and sister say nothing about age; Chinese must choose 哥哥 or 弟弟, 姐姐 or 妹妹.
Japanese makes the same four-way split: 兄 / 弟 / 姉 / 妹 — even the characters are the ones Chinese uses (哥 aside).
Korean also splits by age, and even by the speaker’s sex (형 / 오빠 ‘older brother’ for a man / a woman); Chinese 哥哥 is the same for every speaker.
Hungarian has the same four words: báty ~ 哥哥, öcs ~ 弟弟, nővér ~ 姐姐, húg ~ 妹妹.
Vietnamese anh / chị (older brother / sister) and em (younger, either sex) split by age; Chinese also splits the younger ones by sex: 弟弟 / 妹妹.

blocks.title: 外 ‘outside’ = through a woman of the family
blocks.text: The mother’s parents (外公, 外婆), a daughter’s children (外孙, 外孙女) and a sister’s children (外甥, 外甥女) all carry 外: in the old patrilineal family they belonged to another family line.

blocks.title: One particle for everything
blocks.text: Where German changes mein / meine / meinen, 的 never changes: 我的哥哥, 我的姐姐, 我的书 — one form for every noun, one or many.

blocks.title: Owner first
blocks.text: The owner always comes first: 老师的书 ‘the teacher’s book’, never *书的老师 (that would mean ‘the book’s teacher’).

askYourself: Who is the owner? → owner (pronoun or noun) + 的 + thing: 我的书, 老师的书.
Is the ‘thing’ a family member, my home or my own group (class, school, country)? → 的 is usually dropped: 我妈妈, 我家, 我们学校.
Is it ‘his’ or ‘her’? → 他的 / 她的 — the same sound, only the character differs.
Is it ‘mine, yours’ standing alone? → 我的, 你的: 这本书是我的.
Which relative exactly? → father’s side or mother’s side, older or younger than you (or than the parent), male or female.

traps: *我书 → 我的书: things keep 的.
*的我书, *书的我 → 我的书: 的 comes right after the owner.
他的 and 她的 both sound tā de — only writing shows ‘his’ or ‘her’.
叔叔, 伯伯 and 舅舅 are not interchangeable: father’s younger brother, father’s elder brother, mother’s brother.
堂 cousins are only the children of the father’s brothers; all other cousins are 表.

quiz.why: Owner + 的 + thing; with things 的 stays.
With close family 的 is usually dropped (我的妈妈 is also correct).

quiz.q: Your father’s younger brother is your …
quiz.why: 伯伯 is older than your father; 舅舅 is your mother’s brother; 姑父 the husband of your father’s sister.
All the mother’s brothers are 舅舅.
外 marks the mother’s side; 爷爷 is the father’s father.

quiz.q: The son of your father’s sister, older than you, is your …
quiz.why: 堂 is only for the children of the father’s brothers.
侄子 is your brother’s son; 外孙 your daughter’s son.

quiz.q: In speech, how do 他的书 and 她的书 differ?

notes.text: Greek puts the possessive after the noun as a clitic (το βιβλίο μου ‘my book’) and the owner after it in the genitive (το βιβλίο του δασκάλου); Chinese puts the owner first with 的: 我的书, 老师的书.
Russian мой / моя / моё agree with the thing owned, and the owner follows in the genitive (книга учителя); Chinese 的 never changes and the owner comes first: 老师的书.
Spanish mi / mis agree in number, and de puts the owner after the thing (el libro del profesor); Chinese reverses the order: 老师的书, literally ‘teacher 的 book’.
English ’s already puts the owner first (the teacher’s book ~ 老师的书), and my / your never change — like 我的. The ‘of’ construction is the reverse: ‘the book of the teacher’ is still 老师的书.
French mon / ma / mes agree with the thing owned, and de puts the owner after it (le livre du professeur); Chinese: owner first, 的, then the thing — 老师的书.
German Annas Buch puts the owner first like 安娜的书, but mein / meine / meinen change; 的 never does. das Buch von Anna is the reverse order — Chinese has only 安娜的书.
Hindi puts the owner first with का / की / के (राम की किताब ‘Ram’s book’) — the order of 的 — but का agrees with the thing owned, 的 never does. मेरा / मेरी ↔ 我的.
Persian ezafe puts the thing first: ketāb-e man ‘book of me’; Chinese reverses it: 我的书. Persian can also suffix the owner (ketābam ‘my book’); Chinese has no possessive endings.
Marathi puts the owner first with an agreeing ending (रामचे पुस्तक ‘Ram’s book’, माझी आई ‘my mother’); Chinese has the same order with an unchanging 的, and drops it with family: 我妈妈.
Arabic puts the thing first and changes it (kitābu l-muʿallimi ‘the teacher’s book’) or adds a suffix (kitābī ‘my book’); Chinese leaves the thing unchanged and puts owner + 的 first: 老师的书, 我的书.
Hebrew uses shel after the thing (ha-sefer shel ha-more), a construct form or a suffix (sifri ‘my book’); Chinese puts owner + 的 before an unchanged noun: 老师的书, 我的书.
Turkish puts the owner first too (öğretmenin kitabı ‘the teacher’s book’) but marks both words; Chinese marks only the owner, with 的, and the thing stays bare.
Japanese の is Chinese 的 in all but sound: 私の本 ~ 我的书, 先生の本 ~ 老师的书 — owner first, one unchanging particle.
Korean 의 works like 的 (나의 책 ~ 我的书), and Korean too leaves it out with family and one’s own group: 우리 엄마 ‘my / our mum’ ~ 我妈妈, 我们老师.
Finnish marks the owner with -n and the thing with a possessive suffix (minun kirjani ‘my book’); Chinese only adds 的 to the owner: 我的书.
Hungarian marks the thing owned (a tanár könyve ‘the teacher’s book’, könyvem ‘my book’); Chinese marks the owner with 的 and leaves the thing alone: 老师的书.
Swahili puts the thing first with an agreeing ‘of’ (kitabu cha mwalimu ‘the teacher’s book’, kitabu changu ‘my book’); Chinese puts the owner first with an unchanging 的: 老师的书, 我的书.
Luganda puts the thing first with an agreeing possessive (ekitabo kyange ‘my book’, ebitabo byange ‘my books’); Chinese puts the owner first, and 的 never changes: 我的书.
Vietnamese puts the owner after the thing, with của (sách của tôi ‘my book’) or without it (mẹ tôi ‘my mother’); Chinese reverses the order: 我的书, 我妈妈.
Inuktitut marks the owner with a case ending and the thing with a possessive ending — ‘my mother’ is one word, anaanaga. Chinese uses separate words: 我(的)妈妈.

seeAlso.note: German possessives agree with the noun (mein Bruder, meine Schwester, meinen Bruder); Chinese has one unchanging 的 after the owner.
Arabic attaches a suffix to the noun (كِتَابِي ‘my book’, أُمِّي ‘my mother’); Chinese puts the owner first: 我的书, 我妈妈.
Hebrew puts שֶׁלִּי after the noun (הַסֵּפֶר שֶׁלִּי) or a suffix on it (אִמִּי); Chinese 我的 comes before the noun.
